tldr: The headline layer is almost uniformly locked on the bilateral deadlock: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz deal, Iran holds firm on conditions. The most distinctive divergences are India's militaristic framing ('Ready to inflict greater damage on US', 'Iran vows to fight back'), the Breitbart/France 24 pair that surfaces post-midterm strike resumption at title level, and the UK/Pakistan/Southeast Asia cluster that foregrounds Iran's 'only diplomacy can solve this' counter-narrative. Iran state media uniquely presents Araghchi's UNGA meetings as a broad diplomatic rollout rather than a single Hormuz proposal.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only headline in the corpus to state explicitly that Trump 'Expects to Renew Strikes After Midterms', converting what all other outlets frame as a rejection into a scheduled military timeline.
Leads at homepage level with an Iranian threat quote — ''Ready to inflict greater damage on US'' — the only outlet to open with Iranian defiance language rather than the deal-rejection narrative.
Only outlet to foreground Trump renaming the strait in the headline ('imagen del estrecho de Ormuz con su nombre'), a territorial-branding provocation absent from all other corpus titles.

Frames Iran's proposal as 'dangling a deal' that could extricate Trump politically — the only headline that attributes strategic agency to Tehran rather than treating the offer as a ceasefire request.

bottom_line: Headline coverage across 20 buckets paints uniform deadlock — Trump rejected the seven-day plan, Iran stands firm — with India uniquely leading on Iranian threat language, Breitbart alone naming post-midterm strikes in its title, and UK/Pakistan/Southeast Asian outlets amplifying Iran's diplomacy-only counter-narrative that body coverage buries below the rejection lede.
